topic: Day 2 · Diabetes Drugs in Acute Illness — What to Hold and Why
speakerTitle: Consultant in Acute Internal Medicine & Diabetes
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: Acute physician with a dual interest in diabetes who runs the AMU medication-reconciliation teaching and believes most inpatient diabetes harm is written on the drug chart before the patient ever gets sicker.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is admitted with pyelonephritis and dehydration. His creatinine has doubled — a clear acute kidney injury. The admitting team treat the sepsis beautifully: fluids, antibiotics, cultures. But nobody touches his regular medications, and his metformin, 1 g twice daily, keeps being handed out. Forty-eight hours later he is confused and breathless with a pH of 6.9, a lactate of 11, and a bicarbonate that has fallen off the bottom of the assay. This is metformin-associated lactic acidosis — and it was entirely preventable by a single instruction on the drug chart: hold the metformin. Today is about which diabetes drugs to stop the moment a patient becomes acutely unwell, and exactly why.

1 · 🧠 The governing principle — acute illness changes the risk of every diabetes drug

A diabetes drug that is perfectly safe in a stable outpatient can become dangerous the instant that patient is septic, dehydrated, hypoxic, fasting, or in AKI. The reasons cluster into a few mechanisms:

  • Reduced renal clearance → drug accumulation (metformin, sulfonylureas).
  • Tissue hypoperfusion / hypoxia → lactate generation the liver cannot clear (metformin).
  • Reduced/absent oral intake → hypoglycaemia from secretagogues; euglycaemic ketosis from SGLT2 inhibitors.
  • Catabolic, insulin-deficient stress state → ketogenesis if insulin is stopped, or if an SGLT2 inhibitor drives it.
When a diabetic patient becomes acutely unwell, the question is not "what is their sugar?" but "which of their drugs is now unsafe?" Reach for the drug chart before you reach for reassurance.
💡 The one thing you must NOT stop

Everything in this lecture is about holding oral agents and some injectables during acute illness. The exception that proves the rule: never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes. Stopping oral drugs prevents harm; stopping basal insulin in a type 1 causes DKA. Hold the tablets, protect the basal.

2 · 💊 METFORMIN — lactic acidosis and when to hold

Metformin is renally cleared and inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis partly by shifting toward anaerobic lactate metabolism. In a well patient with good kidneys this is trivial. In a patient who is underperfused, hypoxic, or losing renal clearance, metformin accumulates and lactate is generated faster than the liver can clear it → metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA): a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with a very high lactate, carrying substantial mortality.

Hold metformin when…Why
Acute kidney injury / rapidly rising creatinineLoss of the sole clearance route → accumulation
Sepsis / shock / any hypoperfusionAnaerobic metabolism generates lactate the liver can't clear
Significant hypoxia (severe pneumonia, decompensated heart failure)Drives lactate production
Dehydration / vomiting / diarrhoeaPre-renal AKI risk → accumulation
Iodinated contrast (if eGFR reduced or AKI risk)Contrast-associated AKI can precipitate accumulation → withhold around the procedure and restart when renal function confirmed stable
Before major / emergency surgery, or fasting/NBMPerioperative hypoperfusion and AKI risk
⚠️ Recognising MALA

Suspect it in any metformin-treated patient with an unexplained high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and a markedly elevated lactate, especially with AKI. It can be lethal; treatment is aggressive resuscitation, treating the precipitant, and — in severe cases — haemodialysis, which clears both the lactate and the metformin. The best treatment is prevention: hold the drug at the first sign of AKI, sepsis or hypoperfusion.

3 · 💊 SGLT2 INHIBITORS — euglycaemic DKA and the sick-day rule

The "-flozins" (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin) block renal glucose reabsorption. During acute illness, fasting, dehydration or surgery they can precipitate euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis — a ketoacidosis in which the glucose is normal or only mildly elevated, so it is missed unless you check ketones. The mechanism: relative insulin deficiency + glucosuria-driven volume/carbohydrate loss shifts metabolism toward ketogenesis, without the tell-tale hyperglycaemia.

⚠️ Euglycaemic DKA — the trap that looks well

An SGLT2-inhibitor patient can be acidotic and ketotic with a glucose of 8–12 mmol/L. If you only screen for DKA when the glucose is high, you will miss it. In any unwell -flozin patient: check blood ketones and a venous gas regardless of the glucose.

  • Sick-day rule: patients are taught to STOP the SGLT2 inhibitor when acutely unwell, not eating/drinking normally, or dehydrated.
  • Surgery/procedures: withhold for at least the day of surgery — guidance commonly advises stopping ~3 days before major surgery / withholding around any procedure requiring fasting — and do not restart until eating and drinking normally and well.
  • Never continue an SGLT2 inhibitor into a fasted or ketotic patient.

4 · 💊 SULFONYLUREAS — hypoglycaemia when intake falls or kidneys fail

Sulfonylureas (gliclazide, glimepiride, glibenclamide) are insulin secretagogues: they force the beta-cell to release insulin regardless of the glucose level. In acute illness two things make them dangerous:

  • Reduced oral intake — the patient stops eating but the drug keeps driving insulin release → hypoglycaemia.
  • AKI — reduced renal clearance prolongs the drug (and active metabolites, especially glibenclamide) → prolonged, recurrent hypoglycaemia that can last many hours and rebound after glucose correction.
💡 Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia is stubborn

Because the drug keeps stimulating insulin, a single ampoule of glucose is often not enough — the patient drops again. Severe sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia frequently needs an ongoing 10% glucose infusion and admission, and in refractory cases octreotide (which suppresses insulin secretion) is the specific antidote. Hold the sulfonylurea in the not-eating or AKI patient.

5 · 💊 GLP-1 RECEPTOR AGONISTS — nausea, gastroparesis and aspiration

GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and dual GIP/GLP-1 tirzepatide) slow gastric emptying and cause nausea. In acute illness this matters in two ways:

  • Aggravated nausea/vomiting and dehydration during an acute illness — they add to GI upset and can worsen a pre-renal picture.
  • Peri-procedural aspiration risk — delayed gastric emptying means a "fasted" patient may still have a full stomach at anaesthesia. Emerging anaesthetic guidance advises caution / withholding around procedures and treating these patients as higher aspiration risk; weekly agents in particular linger.

They rarely cause hypoglycaemia alone but can potentiate it with insulin/sulfonylureas. Hold during significant acute GI illness and factor gastroparesis into any airway plan.

6 · 💊 DPP-4 INHIBITORS, PIOGLITAZONE, and INSULIN

  • DPP-4 inhibitors (the "-gliptins": sitagliptin, linagliptin, etc.) — generally safe to continue in acute illness: low hypoglycaemia risk, weight-neutral, and (with dose adjustment for renal function for most except linagliptin) tolerable. They are the "boring, safe" class — but they also do little in a crisis, so insulin usually takes over glycaemic control anyway.
  • Pioglitazone — causes fluid retention; hold in acute heart failure, fluid overload, or significant acute illness. It has no role in acute glycaemic control and can worsen decompensated heart failure.
  • Insulin — never stop basal insulin in type 1. In type 2, doses are adjusted (often up during stress hyperglycaemia, or switched to a variable-rate IV infusion), but the type 1 basal is sacrosanct. Acute illness is a reason to manage insulin, not to stop it.

7 · 📋 The master hold/continue table

Drug classAcute-illness riskHold or continue?
MetforminLactic acidosis (MALA)HOLD in AKI, sepsis, hypoxia, dehydration, contrast, surgery/NBM
SGLT2 inhibitors (-flozins)Euglycaemic DKA, volume depletionHOLD when acutely unwell, fasting, dehydrated, or peri-operatively
SulfonylureasProlonged hypoglycaemiaHOLD if not eating or in AKI; caution always
GLP-1 / GIP-GLP-1 agonistsNausea, gastroparesis, aspirationHOLD in acute GI illness / around procedures (aspiration risk)
DPP-4 inhibitors (-gliptins)MinimalGenerally CONTINUE (renal dose-adjust); insulin usually takes over anyway
PioglitazoneFluid retention / heart failureHOLD in fluid overload / acute HF / significant illness
Insulin (basal, type 1)DKA if stoppedNEVER STOP — adjust dose / switch to VRIII, but basal continues
💡 Memory hook — "SAD MANS" sick-day drugs to hold

A widely-taught aide-mémoire for oral agents to suspend on sick days: Sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, Diuretics, Metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors. It bundles the diabetes drugs with the other nephrotoxic/volume-depleting agents that together drive AKI. When a patient is vomiting or dehydrated, this list comes off until they recover.

8 · 🩺 Practical inpatient approach

  1. On admission of any acutely unwell diabetic: reconcile every glucose-lowering drug and screen for AKI, sepsis, hypoxia, dehydration, fasting.
  2. Hold metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors up front in AKI/sepsis/hypoperfusion/NBM — do not wait for a complication.
  3. Check ketones in any unwell SGLT2 patient regardless of glucose.
  4. Cover glycaemia with insulin — basal-bolus or a variable-rate IV infusion — rather than reactivating oral agents.
  5. Protect the type 1 basal insulin at all costs.
  6. Document restart criteria: restart metformin when renal function is stable, SGLT2 when eating/drinking normally and non-ketotic, sulfonylureas when reliably eating.
☠️ M&M — the metformin nobody held

A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin 1 g twice daily presented with pyelonephritis, vomiting and a creatinine that had risen from 90 to 210 μmol/L — an obvious AKI. Sepsis care was excellent: fluids, antibiotics, source control. But the medication reconciliation missed his metformin, and it was administered from the ward stock every drug round for two days. As his kidneys failed to clear it, metformin accumulated; with sepsis-driven tissue hypoperfusion generating lactate, he developed a devastating metformin-associated lactic acidosis — pH 6.9, lactate 11, bicarbonate unrecordable — and became obtunded and hypotensive, ultimately requiring emergency haemodialysis to clear the metformin and lactate. He survived a stormy ICU course. Root causes: failure to hold metformin at the first sign of AKI; treating the infection but not curating the drug chart; and no trigger linking "AKI/sepsis" to "stop the nephrotoxic and lactate-generating drugs." One line on the chart — HOLD metformin, AKI — would have prevented the entire event.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Acute illness re-rates every diabetes drug. Curate the drug chart the moment a diabetic patient becomes unwell.
  2. Metformin → HOLD in AKI, sepsis, hypoxia, dehydration, contrast, and before surgery — MALA is preventable and can be fatal.
  3. SGLT2 inhibitors → HOLD when unwell/fasting/peri-operative; check ketones regardless of glucose because of euglycaemic DKA.
  4. Sulfonylureas → HOLD if not eating or in AKI — their hypoglycaemia is prolonged and may need a glucose infusion or octreotide.
  5. GLP-1 agonists → gastroparesis and aspiration risk; hold in acute GI illness and around anaesthesia.
  6. DPP-4 inhibitors are generally safe; pioglitazone comes off in fluid overload/heart failure.
  7. Never stop basal insulin in type 1 — adjust or bridge with a VRIII, but the basal stays.

moderatorQs.q: A septic patient with a rising creatinine is on metformin. Explain the mechanism by which continuing it can produce a life-threatening acidosis.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Metformin is cleared almost entirely by the kidney and it biases hepatic metabolism away from gluconeogenesis and toward anaerobic lactate production. In sepsis you get a double hit: AKI reduces clearance so the drug accumulates, and tissue hypoperfusion and hypoxia generate lactate faster than the liver can clear it. The result is metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA) — a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with a very high lactate and significant mortality. Severe cases need haemodialysis to remove both the metformin and the lactate. The whole cascade is prevented by holding metformin at the first sign of AKI, sepsis or hypoperfusion.

moderatorQs.q: Why is euglycaemic DKA from SGLT2 inhibitors so easy to miss, and how do you protect against it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because the defining clue everyone screens for — a high glucose — is absent. SGLT2 inhibitors dump glucose in the urine, so even as relative insulin deficiency drives ketogenesis and acidosis, the blood glucose stays normal or only mildly raised (often 8–12 mmol/L). A clinician who only checks for DKA when the sugar is high will reassure themselves and miss a patient who is frankly acidotic. The protection is a hard rule: in any unwell, fasting or peri-operative patient on a '-flozin', check blood ketones and a venous gas regardless of the glucose, and follow the sick-day rule of stopping the SGLT2 inhibitor whenever they are acutely unwell, not eating, or dehydrated.

moderatorQs.q: Which common diabetes drug is generally safe to continue in acute illness, and which single one must never be stopped — and why the asymmetry?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) are the class you can generally continue: low hypoglycaemia risk, weight-neutral, and tolerable with renal dose adjustment (linagliptin needs none) — though in practice insulin usually takes over glycaemic control in a sick patient anyway. The drug you must never stop is basal insulin in a type 1 diabetic: they have no endogenous insulin, and withdrawing basal removes the brake on lipolysis and ketogenesis, producing DKA within hours. The asymmetry is the whole theme of the session — holding oral agents prevents harm, but stopping the type 1 basal causes it. You suspend the tablets and protect the basal.

audienceQs.q: A patient on gliclazide who's barely eating keeps dropping their sugars, and after I treat a hypo it comes straight back. What's going on and what do I do?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea — it forces the beta-cell to keep secreting insulin regardless of the glucose, so in a patient who isn't eating it drives prolonged, recurrent hypoglycaemia, and a single shot of glucose is quickly overwhelmed. Hold the sulfonylurea, and rather than repeated boluses start an ongoing 10% glucose infusion with close monitoring and admit the patient, because the effect outlasts a one-off correction. In refractory or severe cases (especially with AKI, or with the long-acting glibenclamide) the specific antidote is octreotide, which suppresses the drug-driven insulin secretion. Do not just keep re-treating hypos and sending them back to the ward.

audienceQs.q: My pre-op patient is on weekly semaglutide. Should I worry about anything on induction?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes — GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide markedly slow gastric emptying, so a patient who has fasted by the clock may still have a full stomach, raising the aspiration risk at induction. Current anaesthetic guidance treats these patients as higher-risk: consider withholding the agent around the procedure (weekly formulations linger for days), assess for residual gastric contents (gastric ultrasound where available), and use aspiration precautions / rapid-sequence induction as appropriate. Also remember it can potentiate hypoglycaemia if combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Factor the gastroparesis into your airway plan rather than assuming standard fasting times apply.

audienceQs.q: The AKI patient's metformin and dapagliflozin are held — when can they safely go back on?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Restart criteria differ by drug. Metformin goes back only when the AKI has resolved and renal function is stable (and the precipitant — sepsis, dehydration, contrast — has passed); check the eGFR before restarting and don't resume into ongoing hypoperfusion. Dapagliflozin restarts only when the patient is eating and drinking normally, euvolaemic, and non-ketotic, because its danger is euglycaemic DKA during fasting/illness. In both cases, document explicit restart criteria on the chart rather than leaving them silently omitted, so the drugs are neither resumed too early nor forgotten at discharge.
